title: Where are you going?
goal: Get around town — ask for directions, take public transport, and finally see **all six place endings** side by side in one table.
bekal: use the six place endings as two parallel sets
name means of transport with the ending *-ga*
ask for directions and understand the answer

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kuidas ma saan Kadriorgu?
dialogs.intro: Budi wants to go to Kadriorg Park and asks a passerby.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, how do I get to Kadriorg?

lines.speaker: Möödakäija:
lines.id: To Kadriorg? Take tram number one.

lines.speaker: Möödakäija:
lines.text: Minge otse, siis paremale. Peatus on seal.
lines.id: Go straight, then right. The stop is there.
lines.literal: go straight, then right-to. stop is-it there.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And where do I get off?

lines.speaker: Möödakäija:
lines.id: At the last stop. Kadriorg is the end of the line.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aitäh! Kas mul on piletit vaja?
lines.id: Thank you! Do I need a ticket?
lines.literal: thanks! question me-at is ticket-part needed?

lines.speaker: Möödakäija:
lines.text: Siis on tasuta. Aga te vajate ühiskaarti.
lines.id: Then it's free. But you need a travel card.
lines.literal: then is free. but you need-you common-card-part.

lines.speaker: Möödakäija:
lines.text: Jah, Tallinna elanikele. Ostke kaart kioskist.
lines.id: Yes, for Tallinn residents. Buy the card at a kiosk.
lines.literal: yes, Tallinn-gen residents-to. buy card kiosk-from.

lines.speaker: Möödakäija:
lines.id: You're welcome. Have a good trip!

notes: ⚠️ **Strangers get *te*, not *sa*.** Look at everything the passerby says: *võtke*, *minge*, *te elate*, *ostke*. With people they don't know, Estonians use the plural as the polite form, like French *vous*. More on this in unit 19.
**Võtke, minge, ostke** are polite command forms. The familiar forms are *võta*, *mine*, *osta*. If you're unsure who you're talking to, the forms ending in *-ke* are always safe.

⚠️ **Parem means both "right" and "better".** You just met the second meaning in unit 14. *Paremale* = to the right, *vasakule* = to the left. Context always tells them apart — and English "right" has double meanings too.

⚠️ **Public transport in Tallinn really is free** for anyone registered as a city resident, including foreign students who register their address. You still have to tap your card on every trip. It's a real policy and one reason the city is so easy for newcomers.

grammars.title: The six place endings — all together, in one table
body: You've used each of them separately since unit 2. This is the first time all six stand side by side, and the layout turns out to be very neat: two sets, three directions each.
after: **Read this table down, not across.** Each column is one complete set, and each row is one direction. Six endings, and none needs to be memorized on its own — all you have to remember is three directions and two sets. (Their names: inessive, elative, illative for the inside set; adessive, ablative, allative for the surface set.)

They all attach to the **genitive**, as promised in unit 6. Now you can see how much one word pair pays off: six place forms, plus *-ga*, *-ta*, *-na*, *-ni* from unit 6. Ten forms from one thing memorized.

⚠️ The surface set is also used for **people**: *mul* (at me, i.e. I have), *mulle* (to me), *minult* (from me). You've been using all of them since units 4 and 5 without knowing they were one family.

grammars.title: By what — the ending -ga
body: One ending covers tools, vehicles and companions all at once.
after: The last row is the only exception you need to know: "on foot" isn't *jalgadega* but *jalgsi*. It's a frozen form of *jalg* (foot).
The *-ga* ending also covers tools: *pastakaga* (with a pen), *noaga* (with a knife), *kaardiga* (by card — you used it in unit 4).
Its opposite is *-ta* (without): *suhkruta* (without sugar), *piimata* (without milk), *minuta* (without me). Very handy in a café.

blocks.title: Places and travel words
items: *peatus* — stop. *bussijaam* — bus station. *raudteejaam* — train station. *lennujaam* — airport. *sadam* — harbor.
*pilet* — ticket. *ühiskaart* — travel card. *tasuta* — free. *edasi-tagasi* — round trip.
*väljuma* — to get off, to depart. *sisenema* — to enter, to get on. *jõudma* — to arrive. *ümber istuma* — to change (vehicles).
⚠️ The *praam* (ferry) to Saaremaa and Hiiumaa is a normal part of travel in Estonia. If you're planning to visit the islands in summer, book your ferry ticket ahead.

English
rows: Excuse me, how do I get to ...?

blocks.text: ⚠️ The last sentence is useful both ways: you'll say it when someone asks you for directions, and you'll hear it when you ask a fellow newcomer. *Pärit* means "from (originally)".

blocks.title: Directions and positions
items: *paremal* (on the right), *vasakul* (on the left) — notice **-le** for direction, **-l** for position. The surface set again.
*põhi* (north), *lõuna* (south), *ida* (east), *lääne* (west). ⚠️ *Lõuna* also means midday — you met that meaning in unit 8.
